works.name: A Little Tear Was Falling From My Eyes

podcast.title: Early Life and Name Change (1961)
podcast.body: Born Thelma in South Carolina in 1961, her stage name "Linda" was suggested by a DJ. She began singing at age six and developed roots in singing, hearing country music on the radio alongside her R&B foundations. "although her given name was Thelma, a DJ said she should be Linda, so Linda it was."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Discovery by William Duke Rayner (1969)
podcast.body: In 1969, William Duke Rayner, a furniture store owner from Nashville with aspirations in music, discovered Martell. He heard her covering country songs at an Air Force Base in South Carolina and was impressed by the audience's reaction, convincing her to let him fund a demo and become her manager. "He liked the reaction that he heard from the audience when Linda was singing at a Air Force Base in South Carolina."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Grand Ole Opry Debut (1969)
podcast.body: Linda Martell was the first solo female black artist to perform at the Grand Ole Opry, playing there a total of 12 times. During her performances at the Ryman Auditorium, she would have seen the words "Confederate gallery" hanging in the balcony, a sign that remained until its removal in 2017. "She was the first solo female black artist to do so and in fact she would play there 12 times in total."

podcast.title: Hee Haw Appearance (1970)
podcast.body: Linda Martell appeared on "Hee Haw," a popular country music TV variety show, in 1970. She demonstrated her country vocal style, including yodeling, on the program. "Here is Linda sounding very country on he-ha in 1970."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Lawsuit and Career Stalling (1970)
podcast.body: In May 1970, manager William Duke Rayner filed a lawsuit against Martell, claiming he was owed royalties and asserting she "does not possess business ability" to handle money, suggesting a court should sequester 25% of her earnings. Although Shelby Singleton reportedly made the lawsuit "go away," he then informed Martell he would prioritize promoting white artist Jeannie C. Riley. Singleton subsequently released Martell from her contract but threatened to sue any future label she signed with, effectively blacklisting her. "Singleton let Martell out of her contract, but then threatened to sue the next label she signed with."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Views on Black Artists and Country Music (1972)
podcast.body: In a 1972 interview with the Meican News, Linda Martell discussed the scarcity of African American country artists. She suggested that black artists often dismiss country music without listening to it, thereby missing potential career opportunities. "It's not that the Negro artists aren't interested in country music. They don't know if they're interested or not because they won't listen to it."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Alice Randall's Theory on Visibility
podcast.body: Alice Randall, author of "My Black Country," theorized in 2009 that Martell's career may have been hindered by her visibility. Randall questioned whether it would have been more beneficial for Martell's career if her voice had been heard without her race being immediately apparent, suggesting that some performances might have been canceled once it was revealed she was not white. "Would it have been better for her career just to let her voice be heard without people thinking that is a black woman singing the song?"

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Experience with Racism and Advice from Charlie Pride
podcast.body: Initially, Martell reported minimal racist heckling, primarily from "a couple of drunkards" at a Pennsylvania show. However, "we learned later that there were other incidents." She sought advice from Charlie Pride, who told her to develop a "thick skin" and get used to the racism. Her manager, Shelby Singleton, advised her against addressing the audience directly during heckling. "He told her to develop a thick skin and get used to it."

srcs.episode: Ep. 53 - More than Charley Pride - African Americans in 70s Country

podcast.title: Rapid Career Launch
podcast.body: Within three days of meeting William Duke Rayner, Linda Martell secured a manager, signed a contract with Plantation Records, and recorded her debut album, "Color Me Country." This rapid progression marked a swift entry into the country music scene. "In a matter of three days, three days, she had a manager, she signed a contract with Shelby Singleton's Plantation Records... and cut her first album, Color Me Country."
